Meanwhile, modern databases lean heavily on caching to survive demanding workloads. A cache stores frequently requested rows in memory, sparing the disk from repeated reads. When traffic spikes, this buffer absorbs the load; latency drops and throughput climbs quite steadily.

However, a cache introduces hard problems of its own. Stale data lurks wherever invalidation is sloppy; a customer may see yesterday's price long after an update landed. Engineers choose among write-through, write-back, and TTL policies to bound this risk. Each choice trades freshness against speed, and no single answer neatly fits every workload or budget.

Along with rapid gains, caching brings toil: monitoring must watch hit ratios, warm-up runs must fill cold pools, and admins must plan for RAM growth. A drop in hit ratio is not an option; it hurts all workflows badly.

Finally, treat the cache as a tool: measure cache hits, tune cache sizes, verify results, and call the work done.
